content: The estimated number of new hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections in the United States, after accounting for underreporting and asymptomatic cases, decreased significantly from approximately 232,000 in 1990 to about 51,000 in 2005. The incidence rate dropped to 4 per 100,000 population, and racial and ethnic disparities in HBV incidence were nearly eliminated for Asians/Pacific Islanders, American Indians/Alaska Natives, and Hispanics. However, in 2005, the incidence rate among Black individuals remained nearly three times higher than that of other racial and ethnic groups. Individuals who have immigrated to the United States from countries where HBV is endemic are disproportionately affected by chronic HBV infection. The majority of chronic HBV cases in the United States occur among Asians/Pacific Islanders. The prevalence of chronic HBV infection among immigrants from Central and Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Africa ranges from 5% to 15%, reflecting the patterns of HBV infection in their countries of origin. Between 1994 and 2003, approximately 40,000 immigrants with chronic HBV infection were admitted annually to the United States for permanent residence. The hepatitis B vaccine is available in both single-antigen formulations and fixed combinations with other vaccines. The vaccine antigen can be derived either from the plasma of individuals with chronic HBV infection or produced using recombinant DNA technology. In the United States, recombinant DNA technology is used to express the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in yeast, which is then purified using biochemical and biophysical separation techniques. Licensed hepatitis B vaccines in the United States contain 10–40 µg of HBsAg protein per milliliter. These vaccines are free of thimerosal and contain minimal residual mercury from the manufacturing process. Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) is used as an adjunct to the hepatitis B vaccine for postexposure prophylaxis to prevent HBV infection. For individuals who do not respond to hepatitis B vaccination, HBIG alone serves as the primary means of protection after HBV exposure. HBIG is prepared from the plasma of donors with high concentrations of anti-HBs antibodies. The plasma is rigorously screened to exclude donors who test positive for HBsAg, HIV antibodies, hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibodies, or HCV RNA. There is no evidence to suggest that HBV, HCV, or HIV has ever been transmitted through commercially available HBIG in the United States. Commercially available HBIG in the United States does not contain thimerosal. Primary vaccination for adults consists of three intramuscular doses of the hepatitis B vaccine. The standard 3-dose series, administered at 0, 1, and 6 months, induces a protective antibody response in approximately 30%–55% of healthy adults after the first dose, 75% after the second dose, and more than 90% after the third dose. However, the proportion of individuals achieving a protective antibody response declines with age. After age 40, the response rate falls below 90%, and by age 60, only about 75% of vaccinated individuals develop protective antibody levels.
